script.title: Why the Army Bet on Camels

lines: An Army officer marched camels about 85 miles across Texas without water.
He was testing if they could survive.
In 1853, Jefferson Davis became Secretary of War.
He saw the Southwest as a great desert.
The Army needed better transport there.
Major Henry Wayne sailed to the Mediterranean to buy camels.
In 1856, 34 camels landed in Texas.
A second voyage brought 41 more.
In 1857, Edward Beale took 25 camels on a road survey.
Each camel carried 600 pounds.
Beale said he would rather have one camel than four mules.
Congress was asked to buy 1,000 more, but did not act.
In 1859, Lieutenant Hartz ran that dry test.
The camels showed no desire for water.
The horses and mules were distressed.
The camels were not.
Camels like these can drink as seldom as once every 10 days.
You see, it's like filling your car once, then driving all week.
But Davis left to lead the Confederacy.
The Army ran on horses and mules.
Its soldiers lacked camel skills.
In 1864, the camels were sold at auction.
The last one was reportedly seen in Arizona in 1891.
A loose camel may have inspired the Red Ghost legend.

claims.claim: Davis found the Army needed to improve transportation in the southwestern US, which he and most observers thought a great desert; he was appointed Secretary of War in 1853.

Major Wayne and Porter procured camels in the Mediterranean, with stops including Tunisia, Malta, Greece, Turkey and Egypt; on May 14, 1856, 34 camels were unloaded at Indianola, Texas; a second voyage returned with 41 camels, and the Army then had 70 camels.

In 1857, Edward Beale took 25 pack camels on a wagon road survey; each camel carried a load of 600 pounds; Beale said he would rather have one camel than four mules; Floyd recommended Congress buy an additional 1,000 animals, but Congress did not act.

In 1859, Lieutenant Hartz commanded an escort with 24 camels and 24 mules; to test the camels' ability to survive without water they traveled about 85 miles, and the camels showed no desire for water; at Fort Davis the horses and mules were distressed, but the camels were not.
The dromedary camel can drink as seldom as once every 10 days even under very hot conditions.

The experiment failed partly because Jefferson Davis left to become President of the Confederacy, and the Army was a horse-and-mule organization whose soldiers lacked the skills to control camels; the camels were sold at auction in 1864.
The last of the animals from California was reportedly seen in Arizona in 1891; a released camel or a descendant is believed to have inspired the Arizonan legend of the Red Ghost.

cast.hartz: a 25 year old US Army lieutenant, slim build, a boyish freckled clean shaven face, short straw blond hair, a dark blue forage cap, a short dark blue shell jacket with yellow trim, sky blue trousers, 1850s
cast.davis: a 45 year old American statesman, gaunt hollow cheeks, high cheekbones, thin lips, clean shaven, short dark brown hair brushed back, cold grey eyes, a black frock coat and a black silk cravat, 1850s
cast.wayne: a 40 year old US Army major, stocky build, a round sunburnt face, sandy hair, a full reddish brown beard, a long dark blue frock coat with two rows of brass buttons and gold shoulder straps, 1850s
cast.beale: a 35 year old American frontier surveyor, tall and lean, long wavy black hair to his collar, a thick black moustache, a wide brimmed tan felt hat, a fringed buckskin jacket over a red flannel shirt, 1850s
cast.driver: a 40 year old Turkish camel driver, a weathered olive face, a thick black moustache, a red felt fez, a striped red and blue vest over a white shirt, baggy brown trousers, 1850s
